one_liner: Research generator of CRC32-hashed perfect hash tables for 80 JS/TS keywords; beats gperf ~1.2-1.4x except on keyword-only input.
what_it_does: A research repo, not a library. It generates C++ perfect-hash lookup functions for a fixed set of 80 JavaScript/TypeScript keywords, then benchmarks them against gperf 3.1 option combos, a Python rewrite of gperf's output (mygperf), binary and linear search, frozen::unordered_map, std::unordered_map, and Rust phf and HashMap. generate-pht.cpp takes flags (--hasher, --characters, --table-size, --string-compare, --cmov, ...) and emits a .cpp that exports `token_type look_up_identifier(const char*, size_t) noexcept`; each variant is built as a shared library that the Google Benchmark harness loads with dlopen. The keyword list is compiled into the generator from token.h, so there is no gperf-style input file.
how_it_is_fast: Stock gperf hashes with len + asso_values[s[0]] + asso_values[s[1]] + asso_values[s[len-1]]. The winning pht variant instead packs four selected bytes (first two and last two) into one 32-bit word and hashes it with a single SSE4.2 CRC32 instruction (_mm_crc32_u32). The generator brute-forces the seed and table size until all 80 keys land in distinct slots (a perfect hash: one probe, no collision chain); the --table-size=small search settled on 262 slots. A lookup rejects lengths outside 2..11, compares the first character, memcmps the rest, and checks the length by reading the NUL at entry_keyword[size], with keywords stored inline in 13-byte entries instead of gperf's default const char* pointers. Other variants try SIMD compares (SSE2 movemask, PTEST, PCMPESTRM, NEON), cmov-based branchless result selection, and AES, Lehmer-128, xxHash3, FNV-1a and Pearson hashers.
when_to_use: You write a lexer and want to know how to beat gperf on a small fixed keyword set (here 80 keys of 2-11 bytes); read generate-pht.cpp and the committed generated/ outputs as a worked design study.

Your lookups are mostly misses (identifiers that are not keywords). The length bounds check plus the first-character check rejected them fastest: ~69 us vs ~95 us for stock gperf on the non-keyword corpus.
You target x86-64 with SSE4.2. The winning hasher is the CRC32 instruction, and the Makefile builds the icrc32 variants only on Linux x86-64.
You want a ready harness that compares gperf options, frozen::unordered_map, std::unordered_map, binary/linear search and Rust phf on one key set, using Google Benchmark and perf stat.
when_not_to_use: Anything you ship or modify. LICENSE is CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 and README says 'EDUCATIONAL USE ONLY', so commercial use and derivatives are not allowed.
Keyword-heavy input. On the keywords-only corpus gperf was only 'competitive' with the best pht variant, so expect no win there.
A plain memcmp compare. Every pht hasher with --string-compare=memcmp lost to gperf on all three corpora; the gain comes from the check1memcmp compare.

Key sets that change at runtime or come from a file. Keys are compiled in from token.h, there is no insertion, and the generator exits with 'character selection is not unique' if the chosen characters do not tell the keys apart.
Non-x86-64 or big-endian targets for the winning config. icrc32 needs the SSE4.2 CRC32 intrinsic, and pht.h has a FIXME noting that its 2-byte memcpy character load is endian-dependent.

integration.dependencies: Generated lookups: pht.h, fnv.h, token.h, and the xxHash header (pht.h includes <xxhash.h> unconditionally). Full harness: Google Benchmark, gperf 3.1, frozen, Python 3, and Rust/cargo (phf crate). The Makefile hard-codes local paths such as ~/tmp/Projects/xxhash, ~/tmp/Projects/frozen/include and ~/Toolchains/clang-stage2.
integration.min_toolchain: C++20 plus GNU extensions (__uint128_t, [[gnu::always_inline]], GNU inline asm for the --cmov variants). The author built with g++-12 and a local clang build on Linux and with make's default compiler on macOS; MSVC is not addressed.
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 with SSE4.2 and AES-NI (-msse4 -maes) for the icrc32, aes and SIMD-compare variants; macOS aarch64 for the lehmer128, fnv1a32, pearson8 and NEON variants. Little-endian assumed. The generator needs getopt_long_only and the harness needs dlopen.
integration.thread_safety: not documented; each generated look_up_identifier reads only constexpr tables and keeps no mutable state

gotchas: The SIMD compare variants (sse2, ptest, cmpestri, neon-mask-test) load 16 bytes, and chunk84 loads 12 bytes, from the input pointer whatever the key length. The harness pads every buffer by 32 bytes (padding_bytes in token.h). The check1memcmp winner reads only `size` input bytes.
--no-early-bounds-check read past the end of the table through entry_keyword[size] (issue #1). It is safe only together with --keyword-size-in-entry, which is how the Makefile pairs them.

The 'gperf --inline-strings' baseline is not a stock gperf 3.1 option. The Makefile strips the flag and defines GPERF_INLINE, which changes token.gperf's struct to inline char arrays. mygperf is a Python post-processor of gperf's tables with the author's compare code.
Source files carry GPL-3.0-or-later 'part of quick-lint-js' headers, while README and LICENSE say CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0, and issue #3 about licensing is still open. Treat the code as read-only reference.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Pick this repo to learn why a gperf-class keyword table is fast or slow: it ablates hasher, character selection, table size and compare strategy against gperf 3.1 options and frozen::unordered_map on one workload. For code you can ship, use triehash (also benchmarked against gperf) or frozen (a constexpr C++ container API), after you check their licenses, because this repo forbids derivatives.
verified_claims_summary: The author's dev log (notes.txt: rounded '~' figures, no raw output) gives time per benchmark iteration, where one iteration looks up every identifier in a ~287 KB corpus built from jquery-3.5.1.js. pht icrc32 + check1memcmp took ~69 us vs ~95 us for stock gperf 3.1 on non-keywords (~1.38x) and ~152 us vs ~188 us on mixed (~1.24x; ~1.21x vs gperf with inline strings), and only tied gperf on keywords-only. Builds are -O3 -std=c++20 with g++-12 or a local clang on Linux x86-64; notes.txt names no CPU or compiler for these figures, and the Ryzen 9 5950X appears only in its perf-stat section.
status_note: Abandoned since 2023-03-12 (not archived, 2 open issues) and licensed CC-BY-NC-ND-4.0 'EDUCATIONAL USE ONLY', so read it rather than vendor it; the author's maintained GPL-3.0 descendant of the technique is quick-lint-js's tools/generate-lex-keyword.cpp, which hashes the first two and last two characters with a multiply-shift into a power-of-two table.
